platforms.title: 4 Signs Lower Right Belly Pain Could Be Appendicitis
platforms.meta_description: Lower right belly pain is usually harmless, but appendicitis has a pattern: it starts mid-tummy, moves right and builds. The signs, and when to call 111 or 999.
platforms.body_html:
A dull ache around the belly button that you put down to something you ate, then, a few hours later, a sharper pain low on the right side. That sequence is the one doctors listen for. According to the NHS, appendicitis usually starts with pain in the middle of the tummy that moves to the lower right side after a few hours. Most pain in that corner turns out to be something else, such as trapped wind, constipation, a strained muscle or, in women, an ovarian cyst. What separates the harmless from the urgent is how the pain behaves over time.

Why the Pain Moves Instead of Starting on the Right

The appendix is a narrow, finger-shaped pouch hanging off the large bowel, closed at one end. When its opening gets blocked, pressure and bacteria build up inside a dead-end tube and it starts to swell. At that stage the signal travels along the same vague gut nerves that serve the whole middle of the abdomen, so the brain registers a poorly placed ache near the navel. Once the inflammation reaches the lining of the abdominal wall right next to the appendix, sharper, well-mapped nerves take over and the pain lands in the lower right corner. That is why walking, coughing or going over a bump in a car hurts: every jolt moves an inflamed lining.

Four signs together raise the suspicion. First, pain that started centrally and then moved to the lower right. Second, pain that gets worse when you move, cough or press on the spot. Third, loss of appetite, often with nausea or vomiting. Fourth, a mild temperature. The NHS notes appendicitis is most common in children over 10 and young adults and rare in babies under 12 months, and that the pain can be milder, slower to develop or in a different place in pregnancy, in young children and in older people. Missing the textbook picture does not rule it out.

Get Checked the Same Day, and Let Someone Else Drive

The NHS advice is graded. Get urgent advice from a GP or NHS 111 if the pain is gradually getting worse, does not go away, or moves to the lower right side. Call 999 or go to A&E if the pain is severe, or if you notice confusion, blotchy or pale skin, or difficulty breathing, which can be signs of sepsis. The NHS also says not to drive yourself to A&E; ask someone to take you, or call 999, and bring any medicines you take.

The urgency has a reason. If an inflamed appendix bursts, the NHS warns it can cause peritonitis, an infection of the lining of the abdomen, as well as sepsis, an abscess or a bowel blockage, all of which need urgent surgery and antibiotics. A sudden easing of pain is not automatically good news here, because pain can briefly ease when the appendix ruptures before the infection spreads.

A common worry is that a painkiller will mask the problem. The NHS itself says to take painkillers if you need them, and a Cochrane review (Manterola and colleagues, 2011) of eight randomised trials found that opioid pain relief for adults with acute abdominal pain did not increase the risk of diagnostic or treatment errors. Pain relief is not the danger. The danger is using it as a reason to sit at home overnight while the pain keeps building.

In hospital, diagnosis usually combines an examination, blood tests and often an ultrasound or CT scan. Treatment is usually keyhole surgery, which the NHS says takes about an hour, with most people recovering within one to two weeks. Antibiotics alone are sometimes offered if the infection has not spread. In the Finnish APPAC randomised trial (Salminen and colleagues, JAMA 2018), adults aged 18 to 60 with CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis who were treated with antibiotics had a cumulative recurrence of 39.1% at five years, so roughly six in ten avoided an operation over that period. It is a genuine option, but one to weigh with a surgeon rather than a reason to delay assessment.

Moving, Building Pain Is the Signal

No single symptom proves appendicitis. The pattern is what counts: a central ache, a move to the lower right, pain that worsens with movement, no appetite, a raised temperature. If two or three of those line up and the pain is building over hours rather than fading, that is a same-day assessment, not a wait-and-see. If the ache is still there this evening, try one simple check: walk across the room and cough once. If either sends a sharp jolt to the lower right, call NHS 111 or your GP now rather than waiting for the morning.

Sources

  • NHS. Appendicitis (nhs.uk)
  • Manterola C, et al. Analgesia in patients with acute abdominal pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2011
  • Salminen P, et al. Five-Year Follow-up of Antibiotic Therapy for Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis in the APPAC Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA, 2018
